extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists who write, read, or referee mathematical proofs (authors, students, and referees)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical method for writing mathematical proofs using hierarchical structuring (named steps, numbered levels, Assume/Prove, Proof Sketch, Case constructs) so proofs are easier to read, verify, and debug. Emphasizes how much detail to give, numbering/abbreviation conventions, and reader-oriented presentation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical structuring (structured proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method, based on hierarchical structuring, organizes a proof into named, numbered steps at multiple levels so the structure of the proof is manifest and readers can inspect only the level(s) they desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes it much harder to prove things that are not true; refines natural deduction for ordinary mathematics; allows readers to see a high-level outline and drill into lower-level detail. Structured proofs accommodate as much detail as desired and make obvious when steps are omitted. Use hierarchy to manage complexity; be aware structured proofs look intimidating until one is used to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use names for variables and explicit structure in statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof steps and statements should use named variables (e.g., x, y, z, n) and show structure explicitly instead of burying expressions in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variables with names and structured formulas are easier to read and less error-prone than prose descriptions. The brevity and manifest structure of formulas (e.g., xn + yn = zn) aids comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a Proof Sketch (road map) before the structured proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a Proof Sketch: an informal explanation of the following proof that gives intuition and shows how lemmas are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Proof Sketch serves as a 'road map' helping readers understand why the proof works; it can point out uses of lemmas or non-obvious connections not immediately apparent from the high-level step list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use explicit Assume: and Prove: clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: After the proof sketch, state clearly the assumptions and the goal using Assume: and Prove: clauses (e.g., Assume: 1. r ∈ Q 2. r^2 = 2  Prove: False).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes the hypotheses and target of the proof explicit and numbered, so later references can cite specific assumptions. Treat the theorem as a step with a null string number so assumptions are consistently numbered (e.g., ':1' denotes first assumption of theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbered steps and explicit step references ending with Q.E.D.
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the proof as a sequence of numbered statements (steps) that conclude with Q.E.D. Steps are referenced by number in proofs of other steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of the statements as the left column of a two-column proof (reasons omitted). Numbered steps make justifications explicit; references to steps should obey scoping rules (a step can be used only where its assumptions hold). Use Q.E.D. to denote the assertion proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of thumb for depth: lowest-level statements should be obvious + one more level
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand the proof until the lowest-level statements are obvious, and then continue for one more level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discipline reduces errors: most mistakes come from not carrying the proof to enough levels. Structured proofs can be long; unlike conventional proofs, adding detail does not make the proof confusing. Authors should be skeptical readers of their own proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowest-level paragraph proofs should be short and transparent
rubrics_metrics.description: At the bottom of the hierarchy the paragraph-style proofs must be short, completely transparent, and obvious to the intended verifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a lowest-level paragraph is not obvious, expand further. The goal is that the reader (or referee) should not need to infer hidden steps at the bottom level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use chains of equalities (or transitive chains) for transitive relations
rubrics_metrics.description: For transitive relations (e.g., equality, <, logical equivalence, implication), present proofs as a string of equalities/relations each with a brief justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This style is simple and direct and should be used whenever possible; it clarifies argument flow and avoids hidden leaps of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Let (definitions) to introduce derived variables with explicit definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce variables using Let (or definitional statements) that fix derived quantities (e.g., Let: m ∆ p/gcd(p,q), n ∆ q/gcd(p,q)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions should be explicit and used in lower-level proofs. Lamport notes a preference for using '=' for 'equals by definition' rather than '≡' because '≡' can also mean logical equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact/abbreviated numbering scheme with scoped references
rubrics_metrics.description: For deep proofs abbreviate long step numbers (e.g., represent 3.1.1.1.2 as (4)5)2 or similar) and use scoping rules so an abbreviated reference denotes the most recent step with that number under the current ancestor assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviated numbers save space and remain unambiguous because a step can be used only within the scope (proof of its parent) under whose assumptions it was proved. Use further abbreviation for assumptions (e.g., (5) vs (5):3) as needed. Ensure references obey the rule that a step can only be used where its proof's assumptions hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case construct for proof by cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a Case step as an abbreviation for 'Assume: Statement of assumption. Prove: Q.E.D.' (i.e., Case: Statement of assumption. means open a subproof for that case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case steps make proof-by-cases explicit and flexible; shared higher-level steps can be used in multiple cases. The final Q.E.D. step should explain why the considered cases are exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit tracking of where hypotheses are used
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proofs so that every use of an assumption or proof step is explicit; the proof should make it clear where each hypothesis is applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a properly written structured proof, simple text searching reveals exactly where every hypothesis is used, which is helpful when producing variants of theorems or debugging proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide two versions of proofs for publication and refereeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should provide a very detailed version for themselves, referees, and interested colleagues, and a less detailed (compressed) version for paper publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed proofs can be compressed into paragraph-style proofs for publication by folding lower levels; electronic journals can include full detail and allow readers to suppress details. This balances thoroughness for verification with space concerns in print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt level of detail to audience and reading goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured proofs are preferred by skeptical readers who check for errors; readers who want to skim may prefer better proof sketches or compressed presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For readers who want the main ideas without details, provide a strong proof sketch or annotations highlighting important steps. For printed text, consider layered presentation (high-level proof followed by lower-level proofs) or hypertext for interactive viewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured proofs reduce but do not eliminate errors — discipline required
rubrics_metrics.description: A structured proof format alone will not eliminate errors; proofs must be written carefully with enough detail, and writers must be skeptical of their own arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many published papers contain mistakes; structured proofs make mistakes easier to find. However, lazy writers may resist the extra work required. The author reports repeatedly finding errors when converting conventional proofs into structured form.
